subtopics.title: Pointers & Pointer Arithmetic
subtopics.subtitle: Addresses, & and *, sizeof-scaled arithmetic, void/const pointers, malloc and free

concepts.text: What a Pointer Is

A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Two operators do all the work: & (address-of) yields the address of an object, and * (indirection or dereference) accesses the value stored at an address. A pointer is declared as type *name; the type tells the compiler what kind of object lives at that address, which decides how *p is interpreted and how far p + 1 moves. Reading or writing *p reads or writes the pointed-to variable itself, so a pointer is an alias for another object.

int x = 5;
int *p = &x;                 /* p holds the address of x */
*p = 10;                     /* writes through p: x is now 10 */
printf("%d\n", *p);          /* 10  - the VALUE at the address */
printf("%p\n", (void *)p);   /* the ADDRESS of x, e.g. 0x7ffd3a2c */
printf("%p\n", (void *)&p);  /* address of the pointer variable itself */
int *r = p;                  /* two pointers may hold the same address */
*r = 20;                     /* x is now 20; *p is also 20 */
Declaration and initialisation rules:
items: In int *p, q; the * binds to the name, so p is a pointer but q is a plain int. Write int *p, *q; for two pointers.
A pointer must be given a valid address (&var, another pointer, the result of malloc, or NULL) before it is dereferenced. A declared but never initialised pointer is a wild pointer holding garbage.

NULL (defined in <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h> and <stddef.h>) is a pointer value that points nowhere; it compares equal to 0. Dereferencing NULL crashes the program, so test if (p != NULL) or simply if (p) first.

The size of a pointer depends on the machine, not on what it points to: sizeof(char *) == sizeof(int *) == sizeof(double *), which is 4 bytes on a 32-bit system and 8 bytes on a 64-bit system. sizeof(*p), by contrast, is the size of the pointed-to type.
Pointer types are not interchangeable: assigning int * to double * without a cast is an error or at least a warning, because the two types dereference and advance differently.

concepts.text: Pointer Arithmetic

Arithmetic on a pointer is scaled by the size of the type it points to. p + 1 is the address of the next object of that type, i.e. the numeric address plus sizeof(*p) bytes, so for an int pointer p++ adds 4, for a double pointer it adds 8 and for a char pointer it adds 1. The operators ++, --, +=, -=, + and - with an integer are all defined this way. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them (type ptrdiff_t from <stddef.h>), not the number of bytes, and relational comparison (<, >, ==) of pointers into the same array compares their positions.

rows: p + n, p - n, p++, p--, p += n
Address moved by n × sizeof(*p) bytes
p - q (both in the same array)
p == q, p != q, p < q, p > q
Adding two addresses has no meaning
Multiplication, division and modulus are undefined for pointers
Element size unknown; cast to a concrete type first (GCC treats it as 1 byte)

concepts.text: Tricky forms of * with ++ (postfix ++ binds tighter than unary *, and unary operators group right to left):
items: *p++ is *(p++): yields the value p currently points to, then advances p to the next element.
*++p advances p first and then dereferences the new position.
(*p)++ increments the value stored at p; p itself does not move.
++*p is ++(*p): the same as (*p)++ except that the expression evaluates to the incremented value.
*p + 1 is (*p) + 1, an int, while *(p + 1) is the next element; the parentheses change the meaning completely.

concepts.text: void, const and Multi-level Pointers

A void * is a generic pointer that can hold the address of any object type; it cannot be dereferenced or used in arithmetic until it is cast to a concrete pointer type. malloc returns void *, which converts implicitly to any object pointer type in C (C++ requires an explicit cast). A pointer to a pointer, int **pp = &p, stores the address of a pointer: *pp is p and **pp is the int; it is used for dynamic 2-D arrays and to let a function change a caller's pointer. Read const declarations right to left: const int *p is a pointer to a constant int (the pointee cannot be changed through p, but p can be moved), int *const p is a constant pointer to int (p cannot be moved, but *p can be changed), and const int *const p fixes both.

int x = 7, y = 9;
int *p = &x;
int **pp = &p;              /* pointer to pointer */
printf("%d\n", **pp);       /* 7 */
*pp = &y;                   /* changes p itself: p now points to y */
const int *a = &x;          /* *a = 1 is an ERROR, but a = &y is fine */
int *const b = &x;          /* b = &y is an ERROR, but *b = 1 is fine */
const int *const c = &x;    /* neither the pointer nor the pointee may change */
void *v = &x;               /* generic pointer: holds any address */
printf("%d\n", *(int *)v);  /* cast before dereferencing: 7 */
Dynamic Memory in C

Automatic variables vanish when their block ends, and array sizes must be known at compile time in classic C. The <stdlib.h> heap functions remove both limits: malloc(n) allocates n uninitialised bytes, calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes set to zero, realloc(p, n) resizes a block to n bytes keeping its contents (it may move the block and return a new address), and free(p) returns the block to the system. The size is always written as count × sizeof(type) so the code stays correct when the type changes. Heap memory lives until free is called, so it can be returned from functions safely, but every malloc must be matched by exactly one free.

#include <stdlib.h>
int n = 5;
int *arr = (int *)malloc(n * sizeof(int));  /* cast is optional in C */
if (arr == NULL) { puts("out of memory"); return 1; } /* always check */
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = i * i;  /* use like an array */
arr = realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof(int));       /* grow to 10, old values kept */
int *z = calloc(10, sizeof(int));           /* 10 ints, all zero */
free(arr);  arr = NULL;                     /* release, then neutralise */
free(z);                                    /* never free the same block twice */
Pointer pitfalls that MCQs like to test:
items: Dangling pointer: points to memory that has been freed or to a local variable whose block has ended; dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.
Memory leak: heap memory that no pointer references any more (for example, p = malloc(..) twice without free), so it can never be freed while the program runs.
Wild pointer: declared but never initialised; it holds a random address.
NULL pointer: intentionally points nowhere; safe to test, never safe to dereference. free(NULL) is harmless.
Double free and using the old pointer after realloc moved the block are both undefined behaviour.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Pointer Arithmetic and Heap Memory

Pointer arithmetic can be scaled only because every pointer type carries the size of its target. For T *p, the expression p + i is computed as the address in p plus i × sizeof(T) bytes, and p[i] is simply *(p + i). Subtraction runs the same rule backwards: the byte gap between two pointers is divided by sizeof(T), so q − p counts elements, not bytes. These results are guaranteed only while both pointers stay inside one array or at the address just past its last element; forming any other address, even without dereferencing it, is undefined behaviour.

Special cases and common mistakes:
items: p = realloc(p, n) leaks the old block when realloc fails, because the only pointer to it is overwritten with NULL; assign to a temporary and copy it back only on success.
realloc(NULL, n) behaves exactly like malloc(n), and free(NULL) does nothing, so both are safe starting and ending points.
Writing malloc(n * sizeof *p) instead of naming the type keeps the size correct if the declaration of p changes later.
To let a function change which block the caller's pointer refers to, pass the pointer's address (int **); a plain int * parameter changes only a copy.
Relational tests (<, >) are defined only for pointers into the same array; == and != may compare any two valid pointers, or a pointer with NULL.
After free(p) the address left in p is stale; setting p = NULL makes an accidental second free harmless and keeps a later if (p) test honest.

concepts.text: NULL, '\0' and 0 are different ideas that share the value zero. NULL is a null pointer constant meant for pointers, '\0' is the null character (a char of value 0) that ends every string, and 0 is an ordinary integer. Use each in its own context: p = NULL, s[i] == '\0', n = 0.

For address questions, multiply before adding: new address = old address + n × sizeof(T). For pointer differences, divide the byte gap by sizeof(T). Always check whether the question wants elements (q − p) or bytes ((char *)q − (char *)p).

formulas.plainText: p + i → address of p + i × sizeof(*p) bytes
q − p = (address difference) ÷ sizeof(*p), in elements
sizeof(any pointer) = 4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 bytes on 64-bit, regardless of T
bytes to request for n objects of type T = n × sizeof(T)

notes.text: In *p versus p questions, track carefully whether the ADDRESS or the VALUE is being printed or changed. Draw a small memory diagram (variable, address, contents) before answering an output-prediction question.

p++ on an int pointer moves 4 bytes, not 1. If a question shows addresses (p = 1000, then p + 3), the answer is 1000 + 3 × sizeof(int) = 1012 on a typical machine, 1000 + 3 × 8 = 1024 for a double pointer.
Mixing allocation families (malloc with delete, new with free, new[] with delete) or freeing the same block twice is undefined behaviour. Every malloc/calloc/realloc block needs exactly one free.
int *p, q; declares only ONE pointer. Also, %p expects a void *, so cast: printf("%p", (void *)p). Printing a pointer with %d is technically wrong even though it often appears in exam code.

flashcards.front: What is a pointer?
flashcards.back: A variable that stores the memory address of another variable. It is declared with *, given an address with &, and dereferenced with * to reach the value.

flashcards.front: What is a dangling pointer?
flashcards.back: A pointer that refers to memory that has been freed or to a local variable that has gone out of scope. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.

flashcards.front: Difference between const int *p and int *const p?
flashcards.back: const int *p: the int cannot be changed through p, but p may point elsewhere. int *const p: p is fixed to one address, but *p may be changed.

flashcards.front: malloc vs calloc?
flashcards.back: malloc(n) allocates n bytes and leaves them uninitialised; calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes and sets every byte to zero. Both return NULL on failure and must be freed.

questions.questionText: After the declaration int *p, q; which statement is correct?
options: p is a pointer to int and q is a plain int
p and q are both pointers to int
p and q are both plain ints
q is a pointer to int and p is a plain int
questions.explanation: In a declaration the * belongs to each individual declarator, not to the type, so only p is a pointer. Write int *p, *q; to declare two pointers.
*p = *q copies b's value into a, so a = 7. q = p then makes q point to a as well, so *q = 10 overwrites a while b keeps 7.

questions.questionText: Given int x; int *p = &x; which declaration lets pp store the address of p (pp = &p)?
questions.explanation: &p has type int **, so pp must be a pointer to a pointer to int. int *pp[2] is an array of two int pointers, int (*pp)[2] is a pointer to an array of two ints, and int &pp is not valid C.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the null pointer in C is correct?
options: Dereferencing NULL always gives 0, because NULL points to address 0
free(NULL) crashes the program, so it must always be guarded with an if
NULL may be assigned only to pointers of type void *
A null pointer compares equal to 0 (and to NULL), and dereferencing it is undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: NULL is a null pointer constant that may be assigned to any pointer type and compares equal to 0; it points to no object, so dereferencing it is undefined behaviour. free(NULL) is defined to do nothing.

questions.questionText: Why does standard C reject the expression v + 1 when v is declared as void *v?
options: A void pointer can only ever hold NULL
A void pointer cannot store the address of an int or a double
The size of the pointed-to object is unknown, so the step cannot be scaled
A void pointer is read-only and cannot change after initialisation
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic moves by sizeof(*p) bytes, and void has no size. Cast first, for example (char *)v + 1 or (int *)v + 1; GCC and Clang accept void * arithmetic only as an extension that steps 1 byte.

questions.questionText:
The fragment below is compiled as C. Which numbered line causes a compile error?

int x = 5;
void *v = &x;         /* line 1 */
int *p = v;           /* line 2 */
printf("%d", *v);     /* line 3 */
printf("%d", *p);     /* line 4 */
questions.explanation: A void * cannot be dereferenced, because the type of the object it points to is unknown. Lines 1 and 2 are legal in C, since void * converts implicitly to and from any object pointer type (C++ would need a cast on line 2).

options: Compile error: a void * cannot be reassigned to an int address
Compile error: *(int *)v * 2 multiplies a pointer by 2
questions.explanation: A void * may hold any object address, and after a cast to the right type *(double *)v reads 2.5 and *(int *)v reads 7. Unary * binds tighter than binary *, so the second expression is 7 * 2 = 14.
**pp is x, so x becomes 15. *pp = &y changes p itself to point to y, so **pp *= 2 doubles y to 40, and *p now reads y, which is 40.

options: Compile error: NULL cannot be passed to a function
questions.explanation: The pointer q is passed by value, so alloc changes only its local copy p; q stays NULL and the new block is leaked. To change the caller's pointer, pass &q to a parameter of type int **.

options: The program crashes because a is still NULL
questions.explanation: grow receives &a, so *pp = malloc(...) stores the new address in main's a. The block holds 0, 3, 6, 9, so a[1] + a[3] = 3 + 9 = 12 and a[2] = 6.
*pp = q stores y's address in p, so (**pp)++ raises y to 10 and x stays 5. After pp = &q, **pp is y again, and y += x gives 10 + 5 = 15.

questions.questionText: Assume char is 1 byte, int is 4 bytes and double is 8 bytes. The pointers char *c, int *i and double *d all hold the address 1000. Which addresses do c + 3, i + 3 and d + 3 hold?
questions.explanation: Adding n to a pointer adds n × sizeof(pointed-to type) bytes: 1000 + 3 × 1 = 1003, 1000 + 3 × 4 = 1012 and 1000 + 3 × 8 = 1024.

questions.questionText: On a 64-bit system where pointers are 8 bytes, how do sizeof(char *) and sizeof(double *) compare?
options: They depend on the value stored in each pointer
questions.explanation: Both are addresses of the same width, so sizeof(char *) = sizeof(double *) = 8 bytes. The values 1 and 8 are sizeof(char) and sizeof(double), the sizes of the pointed-to types.
q − p counts int elements: 5 − 1 = 4. Casting both to char * makes each step 1 byte, so the same gap measures 4 × 4 = 16 bytes.
*p++ yields a[0] = 10 and then moves p to a[1]. (*p)++ yields the old value 20 and increments a[1] to 21, while p stays where it is.
*++p first moves p to a[1] and reads 15. ++*p then increments the value a[1] to 16 and yields 16; p still points to a[1], so *p is 16.
p[-2] means *(p − 2), which is a[2] = 5; a negative subscript is legal while the result stays inside the array. *(p − 4) is a[0] = 1 and p[-1] is a[3] = 7, so the sum is 8.
sizeof d is the whole array, 4 × 8 = 32 bytes. sizeof p is a pointer (8), sizeof *p a double (8) and sizeof *q an int (4); sizeof does not evaluate *q, so the null pointer is never dereferenced.
sizeof x / sizeof *p = 20 / 4 = 5 elements. p + 1 is still an int *, so its size is 8 bytes, and (p + 4) − (p + 1) = 3 elements, not 12 bytes.

questions.questionText: p and q are int pointers into the same array and n is an int. Which expression is NOT valid C?
questions.explanation: Adding two addresses has no meaning, so p + q is a compile error. An integer may be added to a pointer, and two pointers into the same array may be subtracted (giving elements) or compared.
The loop pairs 2 − 12, 4 − 10 and 6 − 8, adding −10, −6 and −2, so s = −18. After three passes p points to a[3] and q to a[2], so p < q fails and p − a = 3.
Before each test the (p, q) positions are (0, 7), (2, 6), (4, 5) and then (6, 4), which ends the loop, so the body runs 3 times. Only addresses are compared; the array values are never read.
't' is at index 4 of "pointer", so the loop stops with p = s + 4 and p − s = 4. *(p − 2) is s[2], which is 'i'.

questions.questionText: In C, what is the type of the result of subtracting two pointers that point into the same array?
options: ptrdiff_t, a signed integer type defined in <stddef.h>
The same pointer type as the two operands
questions.explanation: The difference is a count of elements that may be negative (p − q when p comes first), so its type is the signed type ptrdiff_t. It is printed with %td.

questions.questionText: Which pointer comparison is always well defined in standard C?
options: p == NULL, where p is any valid pointer
p < q, where p and q point into two unrelated arrays
p + 10 > p, where p points to the first element of int a[5]
p != q, where p is an uninitialised pointer
questions.explanation: Testing a valid pointer against NULL with == or != is always allowed. Relational operators are defined only for pointers into the same array (or one past its end), forming p + 10 beyond a 5-element array is undefined, and an uninitialised pointer must not even be read.

questions.questionText: In the declaration int *const p = &x; what is constant?
options: The value *p: it cannot be changed, but p can point elsewhere
The pointer p itself: it cannot be made to point elsewhere, but *p can be changed
Nothing: const in this position is ignored
questions.explanation: Read the declaration right to left: p is a const pointer to int. p = &y is a compile error, while *p = 5 is allowed.
const int *p protects the pointee, so *p = 5 is illegal but p may move. int *const q fixes the pointer, so q = &y is illegal but *q = 5 is fine.

questions.questionText: Given int x = 1, y = 2; const int *const r = &x; which statement compiles?
questions.explanation: r is a constant pointer to a constant int, so neither r nor *r may be modified. Reading through r is always allowed, which gives z = 1 + 2 = 3.

options: Compile error: s points to const data and cannot be moved
questions.explanation: const char * makes the characters read-only but lets the pointer move, so s += 3 points to "NTER". *(s + 1) is 'T', and 'T' + 1 is 'U' when printed with %c.

questions.questionText: After which fragment is p a dangling pointer?
options: int x = 4; int *p = &x;   /* x still in scope */
questions.explanation: free releases the block but leaves the old address in p, so p now dangles. Setting p = NULL after free removes the danger, and a null pointer or a pointer to a live variable is not dangling.

questions.questionText: Inside a function, the statements int *p; *p = 10; are executed. Which description is correct?
options: p is a null pointer, so the statement safely does nothing
p is a wild (uninitialised) pointer, and writing through it is undefined behaviour
p is a void pointer, so the statement is a compile error
p is a dangling pointer to freed memory, where 10 is stored safely
questions.explanation: A local pointer that is never initialised holds an indeterminate address, and storing through it may corrupt memory or crash the program. Initialise every pointer to a valid address or to NULL.

questions.questionText: Which fragment is free of undefined behaviour?
options: int *p = malloc(sizeof *p); free(p); p = NULL; free(p);
questions.explanation: After p = NULL, the second free(p) is defined to do nothing. Freeing the same block twice, freeing a variable that was never allocated on the heap, and freeing an address that is not the start of an allocated block are all undefined behaviour.

questions.questionText: Which call allocates space for 10 ints and sets every byte of it to zero?
questions.explanation: calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes and zero-fills them. malloc and realloc leave new bytes uninitialised, and malloc(10) requests only 10 bytes.

questions.questionText: What does malloc return when it cannot allocate the requested memory?
options: The address of the largest free block that is available
Nothing, because it waits until enough memory becomes free
questions.explanation: malloc, calloc and realloc report failure by returning NULL, which is why the result should be checked before it is used.

questions.questionText: Which standard C header declares malloc, calloc, realloc and free?
questions.explanation: The heap functions are declared in <stdlib.h>. <malloc.h> is a non-standard header found on some compilers and should not be relied on.

questions.questionText: p points to a block obtained from malloc. What is the risk in the statement p = realloc(p, 1000 * sizeof(int));?
options: realloc always frees the old block first, so its contents are lost
realloc can only shrink a block, never enlarge it
realloc expects a count of elements, so the size requested is 4 times too large
If realloc fails it returns NULL, p is overwritten and the original block is leaked
questions.explanation: On failure realloc returns NULL but leaves the old block allocated, so assigning the result straight to p loses the only pointer to it. Use a temporary: t = realloc(p, n); if (t != NULL) p = t;

questions.questionText: Which statement about realloc is correct?
options: realloc always returns the same address it was given
realloc sets the newly added bytes to zero
realloc may be used to resize a local array such as int a[10]
questions.explanation: Called with a null pointer, realloc simply allocates n bytes. When it enlarges a block it may move it to a new address, the added bytes are not initialised, and it works only on blocks from malloc, calloc or realloc.
calloc zero-fills the block, so the elements are 0, 0, 4, 0 and 12, and their sum is 16. With malloc instead, the untouched elements would be indeterminate.

options: An unpredictable value, because realloc discards the old contents
questions.explanation: The first loop stores 1, 2, 4 and 8 (1 << i), and realloc keeps them. Then p[4] = 8 + 4 = 12 and p[5] = 12 − 1 = 11, so s = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 12 + 11 = 38.
The second assignment overwrites the only pointer to the first 40-byte block, so that block can never be freed. free(p) releases only the 80-byte block, leaving 40 bytes leaked.

questions.questionText: Assume int is 4 bytes. The array int a[10] starts at address 4000, and int *p = &a[2], *q = &a[7];. What are the address held by p + 3 and the value of q - p?
questions.explanation: p holds 4000 + 2 × 4 = 4008, so p + 3 holds 4008 + 3 × 4 = 4020. q − p counts elements: 7 − 2 = 5, which is the 20-byte gap divided by 4.
m is an array of 3 row pointers, and row i holds i + 1 ints with m[i][j] = i + j. The diagonal gives 0 + 2 + 4 = 6, and m[2][0] = 2 + 0 = 2.
Swapping p and q exchanges only the addresses: p now points to b and q to a. *p = *p * 10 therefore changes b to 20, while a keeps 1.

subtopics.title: Pointers with Arrays & Functions
subtopics.subtitle: Array names as addresses, pointer traversal, passing addresses, function pointers

concepts.text: Array Name as a Pointer

In almost every expression an array name is converted to a pointer to its first element: arr is the same as &arr[0]. Because of this, arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i), and by commutativity of + even i[arr] is legal. There are two exceptions where the name means the whole array: sizeof arr gives the total size in bytes, and &arr gives a pointer to the whole array (type int (*)[n]) whose + 1 skips the entire array. An array name is not a variable, so arr++ or arr = p is a compile error, whereas a pointer that holds the same address may be moved freely.

int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
int *p = a;                              /* a decays to &a[0] */
printf("%d %d\n", a[2], *(a + 2));       /* 3 3 */
printf("%d\n", 2[a]);                    /* 3 : legal, same as a[2] */
printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof a, sizeof p); /* 16 and 4 (32-bit) or 8 (64-bit) */
p++;                                     /* fine: p is a variable */
/* a++;   ERROR: an array name is not modifiable */
printf("%d\n", *p);                      /* 2 */
printf("%d\n", *a + 1);                  /* 2 : (*a) + 1, not a[1] */

rows: Only the address; target must exist

concepts.text: Traversing an array with a pointer:
items: for (p = a; p < a + n; p++) sum += *p; uses the one-past-the-end address a + n as a limit; that address may be formed and compared but never dereferenced.
Equivalent index form: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += *(a + i); the compiler generates the same code.
A string is a char array ending in '\0', so char *s = str; while (*s) s++; walks to the terminator and s - str is the length.
Reversing with two pointers: int *lo = a, *hi = a + n - 1; while (lo < hi) { swap(*lo, *hi); lo++; hi--; }

concepts.text: 2-D Arrays and Arrays of Pointers

A 2-D array int m[3][4] is an array of 3 arrays of 4 ints, stored row by row (row-major). The name m decays to a pointer to its first row, of type int (*)[4], so m + 1 skips a whole row of 4 × 4 = 16 bytes. m[i] is the i-th row (itself decaying to int *), so m[i][j] is *(*(m + i) + j), and because rows are contiguous it also equals *(&m[0][0] + i × 4 + j). An array of pointers, char *names[] = {"Ram", "Sita"}, is different: each element is a separate pointer that may point to strings of different lengths (a ragged array), and names[i][j] is the j-th character of the i-th string.

int m[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
int (*row)[3] = m;                 /* pointer to an array of 3 ints */
printf("%d\n", *(*(m + 1) + 2));   /* 6 : m[1][2] */
printf("%d\n", **(m + 1));         /* 4 : m[1][0] */
printf("%d\n", *(&m[0][0] + 4));   /* 5 : linear index 1*3 + 1 */
printf("%d\n", row[1][0]);         /* 4 : row behaves like m */
char *names[] = {"Ram", "Sita"};   /* array of 2 char pointers */
printf("%c\n", names[1][0]);       /* S */

Passing Pointers and Arrays to Functions

C passes every argument by value: the callee receives a copy and cannot alter the caller's variable. To let a function change a variable, pass its address and dereference inside the function; this simulates call by reference and is how scanf, swap and every "output parameter" work. An array argument is passed as a pointer to its first element, so a parameter written int a[] or int a[10] is really int *a: element changes made in the function are visible to the caller, but sizeof(a) inside the function is the pointer size, so the length must be passed separately.
Returning pointers from functions:
items: A function may return a pointer to static or global storage, to heap memory from malloc, or to memory the caller passed in (for example, strcpy returns its destination).
It must never return the address of a local automatic variable: char *f(void) { char s[10]; return s; } returns a dangling pointer because s is destroyed when f returns.
When the function returns a malloc block, the caller owns it and must call free.
A 2-D array parameter must give every dimension except the first: void f(int m[][4], int rows), equivalent to int (*m)[4].

A function pointer stores the address of a function: int (*fp)(int, int) = add; (the & is optional) and is called as fp(2, 3) or (*fp)(2, 3). An array of function pointers implements menu dispatch tables. Strings are handled entirely through char pointers: char *s = "abc" points to a read-only string literal, whereas char s[] = "abc" makes a writable copy; string functions like strlen and strcpy walk the pointer until the '\0' terminator.

concepts.text: Defining and Using Structures

A structure groups variables of different types under one name, forming a record such as a student with roll number, name and marks. struct tag { members }; defines a new type (allocating no memory), and struct tag v; declares a variable of it; the two can be combined in one statement. A variable is initialised with a brace list in member order, or with C99 designated initialisers such as {.roll = 2}, and members are accessed with the dot operator. A whole structure may be assigned to another of the same type (all members are copied, including arrays), passed to and returned from functions, but structures cannot be compared with ==; compare member by member.
Rules for structures:
items: The definition (struct Student { ... };) is a blueprint and occupies no memory; memory is allocated only when variables are declared.
Members may be of any type: scalars, arrays, pointers, other structures, even a pointer to the same structure type; a structure cannot contain itself by value.
Structure tags live in their own namespace, so struct point point; is legal though confusing. Without a tag the type is anonymous and can only be used in that one declaration.
Members are laid out in the order declared, at increasing addresses; the address of the structure equals the address of its first member.
s1 == s2 is a compile error; s1 = s2 copies all members, and array members are copied deep.

sizeof(struct) is at least the sum of its members, but it is often larger because the compiler inserts padding bytes so that each member starts at an address that is a multiple of its alignment (an int at a multiple of 4, a double at a multiple of 8 on most compilers) and the total size is rounded up to a multiple of the largest member alignment so that consecutive elements of an array of the structure stay aligned. The exact result is compiler-dependent, so a question that expects it must state the sizes. Ordering members from largest to smallest minimises padding, and #pragma pack(1) removes it at the cost of slower, unaligned access.

concepts.text: Unions

A union is declared with the same syntax as a structure, but all of its members share the same storage starting at the same address, so its size is that of the largest member (rounded up to alignment). Only the member written most recently holds a meaningful value; reading a different member reinterprets the same bytes. Unions save memory when only one of several alternatives is needed at a time, model variant records (usually paired with a tag field that says which member is live), give access to individual bytes of a value (endianness test) and describe hardware registers.

concepts.text: Enumerations and Bit Fields

An enumeration defines named integer constants: enum Color { RED, GREEN = 5, BLUE }; gives RED = 0, GREEN = 5 and BLUE = 6, each value being one more than the previous unless assigned. Variables of an enum type are stored as int (sizeof is normally 4) and can be used wherever an int is expected, but they make code far more readable than #define constants. Bit fields are structure members declared with a width in bits, such as unsigned int flag : 1; several of them are packed into one int so that flags and small counters use minimal memory. A bit field cannot have its address taken with &, cannot be an array, and its width cannot exceed the size of its base type; the order of bits inside the word is implementation-defined.
The user-defined types of C at a glance:
items: struct: heterogeneous record; every member has its own storage.
union: same syntax as struct but members overlap; size = largest member.
enum: a set of named integer constants; the underlying type is int.
typedef: creates an alias for an existing type; it never creates a new type or allocates storage.
bit field: a struct or union member of fixed bit width, used to pack flags.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Layout Rules, Union Reads and Bit Fields

The compiler lays out a structure with two rules. Before each member it rounds the current offset up to the next multiple of that member's alignment, and after the last member it rounds the total up to a multiple of the largest alignment in the structure. The first rule lets the processor fetch every member in one aligned access; the second keeps every element of an array of the structure aligned, because element i starts at i × sizeof(struct). The first member is always at offset 0, so a structure and its first member have the same address.

padding bytes = sizeof(struct) − sum of member sizes

notes.text: If a question asks conceptually, "structure size = sum of members, union size = largest member" is the expected answer. If it shows code such as struct { char c; int i; } and asks for sizeof, apply alignment: 8, not 5. Check whether the question states the sizes and alignment.
The closing brace of a struct, union or enum definition must be followed by a semicolon. Forgetting it produces confusing errors on the next line.
Writing one union member and then reading another gives the bit pattern of the first, not a converted value. u.f = 1.5; printf("%d", u.i); prints a large integer, not 1.
Structures may be assigned and passed by value (all members copied, array members included), but they cannot be compared with == or printed with a single printf; handle member by member.

formulas.title: Structure size
formulas.plainText: sizeof(struct) ≥ sum of member sizes
formulas.description: Padding for alignment can make the structure larger than the plain sum; struct { char c; int i; } is typically 8 bytes.

formulas.title: Union size
formulas.plainText: sizeof(union) = largest member
formulas.description: All members overlap in one block, so the block only needs to be as large as the biggest member (rounded to its alignment).

formulas.title: Alignment rule
formulas.plainText: each member starts at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment
formulas.description: Explains where padding bytes go: a 4-byte int after a 1-byte char is placed at offset 4, leaving 3 padding bytes.

formulas.title: Enumeration values
formulas.plainText: enum constants count from 0 and each is previous + 1 unless given a value
formulas.description: enum { A, B = 4, C } gives A = 0, B = 4, C = 5.

flashcards.front: Key difference between struct and union?
flashcards.back: Struct members each have their own memory (size ≈ sum plus padding). Union members share one memory block (size = largest member); only the last-written member is valid.

flashcards.front: Why is sizeof(struct { char c; int i; }) usually 8 and not 5?
flashcards.back: The int must start at an address that is a multiple of 4, so 3 padding bytes are inserted after the char. The compiler aligns members and rounds the total up to the largest alignment.

flashcards.front: What does typedef do?
flashcards.back: It creates an alias for an existing type, e.g. typedef struct { int x, y; } Point; lets you write Point p; instead of struct tag p;. It creates no new type and no storage.

flashcards.front: What are bit fields and what restriction do they have?
flashcards.back: Structure members with an explicit width in bits (unsigned int flag : 1;) packed into one integer to save space. You cannot take their address with & or make arrays of them.

questions.explanation: The int must begin at offset 4, so 3 padding bytes follow the char: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8. The plain sum of members (5) ignores alignment padding.

questions.questionText: What does the declaration struct Book { char title[40]; float price; }; do by itself, before any variable of the type is declared?
options: It allocates 44 bytes of memory under the name Book
It declares a variable named Book with two members
It defines a new type (a template); no memory is allocated until a variable of the type is declared
Nothing usable: struct Book cannot be used until a typedef is added
questions.explanation: A structure definition only describes the layout of a type. Memory is reserved when a variable such as struct Book b; is declared, and struct Book can be used directly without any typedef.

questions.questionText:
Which marked line of this fragment causes a compile error?

struct { int a; } x = {1}, y;
struct { int a; } z;
y = x;           /* A */
z.a = x.a;       /* B */
z = x;           /* C */
y.a = z.a + 1;   /* D */
questions.explanation: Every untagged struct definition creates a new, distinct type. x and y come from the same declaration, so y = x is fine, and copying int members is fine, but z has a different (though identical-looking) type, so z = x is an assignment between incompatible types.
When a brace initialiser lists fewer values than there are members, the remaining members are set to 0, even for a local variable. So a = 5, b = 0 and c = 0.
Designated initialisers (C99) set members by name, in any order: a = 1 and c = 3. The member that is not mentioned, b, becomes 0.
A positional value written after a designator initialises the member that follows the designated one, so 8 goes to c. Members that receive no value, a and d, become 0.

options: Compile error: in.y has no initialiser
questions.explanation: The inner braces {2} initialise only the nested structure: in.x = 2 and the rest of it, in.y, becomes 0. The value 3 then goes to the next outer member, b.
sizeof gives the declared size of the array member, 10 bytes, whatever it contains. strlen counts the characters before the terminating '\0': R, a, m = 3.

questions.questionText:
Which marked line of this fragment causes a compile error? (<string.h> is included.)

struct T { int id; char name[10]; } t;
t.id = 5;                  /* A */
t.name = "Asha";           /* B */
t.name[0] = 'A';           /* C */
strcpy(t.name, "Asha");    /* D */
questions.explanation: name is an array, and an array cannot be assigned with =; its contents must be copied with strcpy (line D) or element by element (line C). Assigning to the int member (line A) is normal.
The dot operator binds tighter than ++, so ++s.x means ++(s.x): x becomes 6 and y = 6 × 2 = 12.
e.join is the nested Date {1, 4, 2020}, so e.join.m is 4; e.id is 7. Members of a nested structure are reached by chaining the dot operator.
o.b = o.a copies the value 1 into b; the two nested structures remain separate objects. Changing o.a.v to 9 afterwards does not affect o.b.v, which stays 1.

questions.questionText: In C (not C++), the declaration struct Outer { struct Inner { int a; } in; int b; }; appears at file scope. Which statement is correct?
options: struct Inner is visible only inside Outer and must be written Outer::Inner elsewhere
Defining one structure inside another is a compile error in C
struct Inner can also be used on its own later in the file, because in C the inner tag has the same scope as struct Outer
The member in takes no memory because Inner is defined inside Outer
questions.explanation: C has no class scope for tags, so a structure defined inside another is declared in the enclosing (here file) scope and struct Inner x; is valid later. Outer::Inner is the C++ rule, and in is a real member occupying sizeof(struct Inner) bytes.
struct A is 1 + 3 padding + 4 = 8 bytes with alignment 4. In B: d at 0, 3 padding bytes, a at 4–11, e at 12, then 3 tail padding bytes to reach a multiple of 4: 16.
Every member of a union begins at the start of the union, so all three offsets are 0. Increasing offsets such as 0 8 16 would describe a structure, whose members follow one another.

Structure: a at 0–3, b at 4, 3 padding bytes, c at 8–15, total 16 (13 bytes of data + 3 padding). Union: the members overlap, so the size is that of the largest member, 8, already a multiple of the 8-byte alignment.
X: a at 0, 7 padding, b at 8–15, c at 16, 7 tail padding = 24. Y: b at 0–7, a at 8, c at 9, 6 tail padding = 16. The members are the same; placing the largest first saves 8 bytes.
a at 0, 3 padding, b at 4–7, c at 8, 1 padding so that d starts at the even offset 10, d at 10–11. The end, 12, is already a multiple of 4, so sizeof is 12 (8 bytes of data + 4 of padding).

questions.questionText: On a typical compiler sizeof(struct { int i; char c; }) is 8: the char is followed by 3 padding bytes at the end of the structure. Why is this tail padding added?
options: To leave room for a terminating '\0' after the char member
Because every structure must occupy a multiple of 8 bytes
So that in an array of these structures every element, and therefore its int member, stays 4-byte aligned
Because a char member is always stored in 4 bytes
questions.explanation: Element i of an array starts at i × sizeof(struct); with a size of 5 the int of the second element would sit at offset 5. The size is therefore rounded up to a multiple of the largest member alignment (4), not to a multiple of 8.
Each printf reads the member that was written last, which is always well defined: first u.i = 10, then u.f = 2.5 after the float has overwritten the shared storage.

Both structures begin with an int tag (a common initial sequence), and C guarantees that this shared prefix may be read through either member of the union. u.b.tag occupies the same bytes as u.a.tag, so it is 2.

options: Compile error: the union has no member name
questions.explanation: Members of an anonymous union are accessed as if they belonged to the enclosing structure, so v[k].i and v[k].d are valid. The isInt tag selects the member that was actually initialised: 7 for v[0] and 2.5 for v[1].

questions.questionText: Given union U { int i; double d; };, which declaration stores 2.5 in member d?
questions.explanation: A brace initialiser without a designator initialises the first member, so {2.5} and {.i = 2.5} both store 2 (converted to int) in i. The designator .d names the member to initialise; assigning a double to a whole union variable is a compile error.

options: It is always 1, the most significant byte
It is always 4, because b[0] keeps only the low 8 bits of n
It is 10, the sum of the four bytes
It is 4 on a little-endian machine and 1 on a big-endian machine
questions.explanation: b[0] is the byte at the lowest address of n. A little-endian machine (such as x86) stores the least significant byte 0x04 there and a big-endian machine stores 0x01, so the result depends on the byte order.

questions.questionText: Which statement about unions in C is NOT correct?
options: A union can have a structure as one of its members
A union variable can be assigned to another union variable of the same type
All members of a union can hold independent values at the same time
Every member of a union starts at the same address
questions.explanation: Union members overlap in one block of storage, so writing one member overwrites the others and only one value is held at a time. The other three statements are true.
Member sizes: s = 4 + 1 + 3 padding = 8, d = 8 and arr = 13. The largest is 13, and the union must be a multiple of the alignment of double (8), so 13 is rounded up to 16.

questions.questionText: Given struct F { unsigned int a : 3; } f;, which operation on f.a is NOT allowed?
options: Assigning a value, as in f.a = 5
Using it in an expression, as in f.a + 1
Printing it, as in printf("%d", f.a)
questions.explanation: A bit field need not start on a byte boundary, so it has no address: &f.a is a compile error, and pointers to or arrays of bit fields are impossible. Reading and writing its value is normal.
A 3-bit unsigned field holds 0 to 7 and wraps modulo 2^3 = 8. After 10 increments it holds 10 mod 8 = 2.

a uses 20 bits of the first unit, leaving 12; b needs 20, so it starts a second unit, leaving 12 bits there, which c fills exactly. Two 4-byte units give 8 bytes (the 52 bits would need only 7 bytes, but storage is allocated in whole units).

questions.questionText: What is the effect of the unnamed field in struct F { unsigned a : 3; unsigned : 0; unsigned b : 3; };?
options: It is a compile error, because every bit field must have a name
It reserves zero bits and has no effect on the layout
It makes b a signed field
It forces b to start at the beginning of the next unsigned int allocation unit
questions.explanation: An unnamed bit field of width 0 tells the compiler to stop packing into the current unit, so b begins in a new unit. With 32-bit units the structure becomes 8 bytes instead of 4.

questions.questionText: A date is packed as struct D { unsigned day : 5; unsigned month : 4; unsigned year : 7; };, where year holds the number of years after 2000. What is the latest calendar year that can be stored, and how many bits do the three fields use in total?
questions.explanation: A 7-bit unsigned field holds 0 to 2^7 − 1 = 127, so the latest year is 2000 + 127 = 2127. The fields use 5 + 4 + 7 = 16 bits (on a typical compiler they share one 4-byte unsigned int, so sizeof is 4).

questions.questionText: Which statement about bit fields in C11 is correct?
options: An array of bit fields can be declared, as in unsigned int f[4] : 2;
The width of a bit field may be larger than the number of bits in its type
Whether a plain int bit field (declared without signed or unsigned) can hold negative values is implementation-defined
A pointer of type unsigned int * may point to a bit-field member
questions.explanation: For a bit field declared as plain int, the standard lets the implementation decide whether it is signed or unsigned. Arrays of bit fields, widths larger than the type and pointers to bit fields are all invalid.

questions.questionText: Given typedef struct Node { int v; } NodeT;, which declaration inside main causes a compile error?
questions.explanation: NodeT is an alias for the complete type struct Node, not a structure tag, so struct NodeT names a different, never-defined structure, and a variable of that incomplete type cannot be declared. The other three declarations are valid.

options: Compile error: ItemPtr is not a type
questions.explanation: The typedef defines two names: Item for the structure and ItemPtr for a pointer to it. p points to it, so p->v *= 3 changes it.v from 4 to 12.

questions.questionText:
Which marked lines of this C fragment (inside main) fail to compile?

struct K { const int id; int v; };
struct K a = {1, 10};   /* Line 1 */
struct K b = a;         /* Line 2 */
b.v = 20;               /* Line 3 */
b.id = 2;               /* Line 4 */
a = b;                  /* Line 5 */
questions.explanation: A const member can get its value only through initialisation, so Line 1 and Line 2 (which initialises b as a copy of a) are valid, and Line 3 changes an ordinary member. Line 4 assigns to the const member, and Line 5 assigns the whole structure, which is not allowed for a structure with a const member because it would overwrite id.
B follows A = 3, so B = 4. C is set to 1, so D = 2. F = B + D = 4 + 2 = 6; an enumerator may be defined using earlier ones.

questions.questionText: Which statement about enumerations in C is correct?
options: Two constants in the same enumeration may have the same value
The constants must be listed in increasing order of value
The first constant is 1 unless a value is assigned
Assigning an int that is not one of the listed constants to an enum variable is a compile error
questions.explanation: enum { LOW = 1, ONE = 1 }; is legal, and constants may appear in any order of value. The first constant defaults to 0, and C lets any int value be stored in an enum variable without an error.
MID = 2, so control jumps to case MID and prints M. Without a break it falls through to case HIGH and prints H, and that break leaves the switch before default.
The constants are MON = 0, TUE = 1, WED = 2 and NDAYS = 3, so the array has 3 elements and hours[TUE] is hours[1] = 6. Placing a count constant last is a common idiom.

questions.questionText: Compared with a group of #define constants, what is an advantage of declaring the constants as an enum?
options: enum constants can hold floating-point values such as 2.5
enum constants can be changed while the program runs
enum constants occupy memory, so their addresses can be passed to functions
The compiler assigns successive values automatically, and the names obey C's scope rules
questions.explanation: Enumeration constants are integer constants numbered automatically (0, 1, 2 … unless assigned) and, unlike macros, they have scope and are known to the compiler and debugger. They must be integers, cannot change and have no address.
Structure assignment copies every member, including all 8 bytes of the array n, so b gets its own copy of "Ram". Changing b.n[0] makes b.n "Pam" while a.n stays "Ram".

y = x copies the array a (so y gets its own "dog") but copies only the address in p, so x.p and y.p both point to buf. y.a[0] = 'f' changes only y.a ("fog"), while y.p[0] = 'b' changes buf, which is seen through both pointers ("bat").

questions.questionText: s1 and s2 are variables of the same structure type. Which operation is NOT permitted on them as whole structures?
questions.explanation: C has no equality or relational operators for structures, so s1 != s2 (like s1 == s2) is a compile error; compare member by member. Assignment, sizeof and taking the address are all allowed.

questions.questionText: For struct { int a; char b; } s;, which statement is always true in standard C?
options: The compiler may store b before a in memory
(void *)&s == (void *)&s.a, because there is never padding before the first member
questions.explanation: The first member is at offset 0, so a structure and its first member share the same address. Padding may make sizeof s larger than the sum (typically 8, not 5), and members are always stored in the order in which they are declared.

DBL is the second enumerator, so a.k is 1. b = a copies the whole structure, union included, so b has its own storage: writing b.v.i = 4 leaves a.v.d at 2.5. Every read uses the member last written in that object.

questions.questionText: Why is memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof a) == 0 NOT a reliable way to test whether two structure variables have equal members?
options: memcmp cannot be applied to structures; the call is a compile error
memcmp compares only the first member of each structure
The padding bytes between or after the members may hold different values even when every member is equal
memcmp stops at the first zero byte, like strcmp
questions.explanation: memcmp compares every byte, padding included, and the contents of padding bytes are unspecified, so two structures with equal members can compare unequal. Compare the members one by one instead.

questions.questionText: Only struct item { int n; }; has been defined (there is no typedef). Which declaration inside main compiles in C?
questions.explanation: Structure tags live in their own name space, so a variable may even be called item: struct item item; is legal. In C the tag alone is not a type name (item a; is valid only in C++), struct a is an undefined, incomplete type, and item struct b; is not valid syntax.

subtopics.title: Structures with Pointers, Arrays & Functions
subtopics.subtitle: Arrays of records, -> access, passing and returning structures, heap records, list nodes

concepts.text: Array of Structures

An array whose elements are structures stores a table of records: struct Student s[50]; holds 50 students, and s[i].marks is one field of one record. It is initialised with nested braces, filled and printed with ordinary loops, and searched by comparing a member of each element. Sorting records is done by comparing one key member and swapping whole elements, because s[i] = s[j] copies every member at once. The array occupies 50 × sizeof(struct Student) bytes, padding included.
Pointers to Structures

A pointer to a structure, struct Student *p = &s[0], reaches members either as (*p).roll or with the arrow shorthand p->roll, which means exactly the same. The parentheses are essential in the first form because . and -> have the highest precedence (together with () and []), so *p.roll parses as *(p.roll) and is an error. Incrementing a structure pointer moves it by sizeof(struct), i.e. to the next record, so an array of structures is naturally walked with a pointer. A string member reached through p->name is still an array: it must be copied with strcpy, not assigned with =.

rows: Member x of structure variable s
Member x of the structure p points to
Parsed as *(p.x): dot on a pointer
Dot needs a structure, not a pointer
Element i of the array member name

concepts.text: Passing Structures to Functions

A structure can be passed to a function by value: the whole record is copied onto the stack, so the callee works on a copy and the caller's data is safe, but copying a large record on every call is slow. Passing a pointer copies only an address (4 or 8 bytes), is fast, and lets the callee modify the original through ->; declare the parameter const struct T * when modification should be prevented. Individual members can also be passed like ordinary variables (f(s.marks)). A function may return a whole structure by value, which is the usual way to build and hand back a record.

rows: Small records such as Point, Date
Large records, arrays of records, modification

concepts.text: Dynamic and Self-Referential Structures

Records can be created on the heap when the count is known only at run time: struct Student *list = malloc(n * sizeof(struct Student)); then list[i].roll and (list + i)->roll both address the i-th record, and free(list) releases the whole table. A self-referential structure contains a pointer to its own type: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; }; is the node of a linked list, and a version with left and right pointers is a tree node. The structure cannot contain a struct Node by value (it would be infinitely large) but a pointer to one has a fixed size, so the chain can grow one malloc at a time.
Checklist when structures meet pointers:
items: Use -> after a pointer and . after a structure variable; (*p).m and p->m are interchangeable.
scanf needs & for scalar members (&s.roll) but not for array members (s.name), which are already addresses.
String members are arrays: copy with strcpy(p->name, "Ram"), never p->name = "Ram".
Allocate with sizeof(struct T) or sizeof *p, never a hand-added sum of member sizes, because padding is included in sizeof.
When freeing a linked list, save p->next before free(p); after free the node must not be read.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Record Tables, Arrow Chains and Linked Lists

The arrow operator is a postfix operator, like (), [] and the dot, so it binds tighter than every prefix operator such as ++, --, *, & and a cast. That fixes the meaning of the combinations that appear in output questions: ++p->x increments the member, (++p)->x moves the pointer first, p++->x reads the member of the current record and then moves, and *p->q dereferences a pointer member. The address of member m of record i is computed from the base address, the record size and the member offset, which is why p + 1 always jumps over a whole record, padding included.

yields the old arr[0].x, then increments it
the object that the member pointer q points to

Passing a structure by value copies all of it, including any array member, so a function can change its copy without the caller noticing; a bare array argument, by contrast, always decays to a pointer. An array of structures passed to a function also decays to a pointer to its first record, so the function works on the caller's records. A function may return a structure by value, even one built on the spot with a C99 compound literal such as return (struct P){x, y};, but a returned pointer must point to storage that outlives the call: heap memory, a static object or a record in the caller's array.

Returning the address of a local structure leaves a dangling pointer, because the local record is destroyed when the function returns.
Binary search over an array of structures works only if the array is sorted on the same member that is searched for.

Only the address forms can change the caller's records, and a pointer parameter that is itself reassigned inside the function does not change the caller's pointer.

p->m ≡ (*p).m for a pointer p to a structure
&s[i] ≡ s + i and s[i].m ≡ (s + i)->m

notes.text: *p.x is a compile error because . binds tighter than *: it means *(p.x). Write (*p).x or p->x.

Output questions typically call one function with the structure (by value) and another with its address (by pointer); only the pointer version changes the caller's record. Trace which parameter form each function uses.

Returning a pointer to a structure that is a local variable of the function is a dangling pointer. Return the structure by value, or return a pointer to heap memory or to an element of an array the caller owns.

formulas.title: Array of structures size
formulas.plainText: sizeof(s[n]) = n × sizeof(struct T)
formulas.description: Total memory of a table of records, with the per-record size including any padding.

formulas.title: Arrow operator identity
formulas.description: Both forms read member m through a pointer; the arrow is shorthand and the parentheses in the long form are mandatory.

formulas.title: Record i through a pointer
formulas.plainText: s[i].m ≡ (s + i)->m

flashcards.front: When should a structure be passed to a function by pointer rather than by value?
flashcards.back: When the record is large (copying is slow) or when the function must modify the caller's data. By value copies the whole structure and protects the original; by pointer copies only an address.

flashcards.front: What is a self-referential structure?
flashcards.back: A structure containing a pointer to its own type, e.g. struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; }. It is the building block of linked lists and trees; it cannot contain itself by value.

flashcards.front: How do you create an array of n struct Student at run time?
flashcards.back: struct Student *s = malloc(n * sizeof(struct Student)); then use s[i].roll or (s + i)->roll and free(s) when done. Check for NULL after malloc.

flashcards.front: What happens to p when p++ is applied to a struct Point *p?
flashcards.back: p advances by sizeof(struct Point) bytes to the next structure in an array, not to the next member. In an array of structures this walks record by record.

questions.explanation: f receives a copy, so p.x = 9 does not touch a. g receives the address of a and p->y = 9 changes a.y. The output is 1 9.

arr[2] is the third record {3, 'z'}, so arr[2].a is 3; arr[0] is {1, 'x'}, so arr[0].c is 'x'.

questions.questionText: Given struct Emp { int id; char name[20]; float sal; } e[50];, assume int and float are 4 bytes and 4-byte aligned (no padding is needed, because every member already starts at a multiple of 4). How many bytes does the array e occupy?

The loop keeps the index of the highest marks. At i = 1, 85 >= 70 selects Bina; at i = 2, 85 >= 85 is also true, so Chet replaces her; 60 at i = 3 does not. With > instead of >= the first topper, Bina, would be kept.
One Team is 8 bytes of name plus 3 × 4 = 12 bytes of players = 20 bytes (p starts at offset 8, already a multiple of 4). t holds 2 teams: 40 bytes. t[0].p is an array of 3 players: 12 bytes.

questions.questionText: Given struct Student { int roll; char name[20]; } s[10]; and an int i, which call correctly reads the roll number and name of record i?

p points to a, so p->y = p->x * 2 assigns 3 × 2 = 6 to a.y; a.x is unchanged.
-> binds tighter than ++, so ++p->x increments arr[0].x to 11 and a = 11. In (++p)->x the parentheses move p to arr[1] first, so b = 20.
p++->x is (p++)->x: it reads arr[0].x (1) and then moves p to arr[1]. p->x++ is (p->x)++: it yields the old value of arr[1].x (5) and then increments the member to 6.

subtopics.title: File Operations & Access Methods
subtopics.subtitle: FILE *, fopen modes, character/string/formatted/binary I/O, EOF, fseek, ftell and rewind

concepts.text: Opening and Closing Files

C reads and writes files through the <stdio.h> stream functions. FILE *fp = fopen("name", "mode"); opens a file and returns a pointer to a FILE object that records the buffer, the current position and error flags; it returns NULL when the file cannot be opened (missing file in read mode, no permission, bad path), so the result must always be checked. fclose(fp) flushes the buffer to disk and releases the FILE; it returns 0 on success and EOF on error. Because output is buffered, data written may not reach the disk until fclose or fflush(fp) is called. Three streams are open automatically: stdin, stdout and stderr.

rows: Append: write only at the end
Kept; every write goes to the end
Read anywhere, write at the end

concepts.text: Reading and Writing: Four Function Families

rows: Return EOF (−1) at end or error, so store the result in an int
fgets reads at most n−1 chars, keeps the newline, returns NULL at EOF
Text; fscanf returns the number of items matched or EOF
Return the count of items completed; use with rb/wb modes

concepts.text: EOF is a macro with value −1 returned by fgetc, getc, fscanf and others when the end of the file is reached or an error occurs; it is why the character functions return int rather than char. feof(fp) becomes true only after a read has already failed, so the loop while (!feof(fp)) { fscanf(...); process(); } processes the last item twice; the correct idiom tests the return value of the read call itself. ferror(fp) reports a hardware or logical error on the stream, clearerr(fp) resets both indicators, and perror(msg) prints a system message for the last failure.
Binary Files and Records

A text file stores numbers as sequences of digit characters of varying length, is human-readable and portable, and may translate the newline character on some systems. A binary file stores the exact memory image of the data: a structure written with fwrite always occupies sizeof(struct) bytes, so the n-th record (counting from 0) starts at byte n × sizeof(struct). This fixed-length layout is what makes random access possible; the cost is that binary files are unreadable in an editor and not portable across machines with different sizes or byte order. On Unix the b in the mode is ignored; on Windows it disables the \n to \r\n translation, which would corrupt binary data.
Sequential vs Random Access

Every open file has a position indicator that says where the next read or write happens. In sequential access the program starts at the beginning and each operation advances the indicator, so reaching the 100th record means reading the 99 before it; this suits text files with variable-length lines and log files. In random (direct) access the program moves the indicator anywhere with fseek(fp, offset, origin), where offset is a long byte count and origin is SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR or SEEK_END; the call returns 0 on success. ftell(fp) returns the current byte offset from the start as a long, and rewind(fp) is equivalent to fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET) plus clearing the error and EOF flags. In the "+" modes an fseek or rewind is also required when switching between reading and writing, and in a or a+ mode every write still goes to the end whatever fseek says.

rows: fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END); ftell(fp) gives the file size

concepts.text: Going Deeper: File I/O in Practice

Every FILE stream keeps a buffer, a position indicator and two status flags, end-of-file and error. Output functions first copy data into the buffer, which is written to the file when it fills, when fflush(fp) or fclose(fp) is called, or when main returns or exit() is called; a crash or abort() can lose buffered data. The position indicator counts bytes from the start of the file and advances with every successful read or write, which is why ftell reports data that may still be sitting in the buffer. Input functions set the end-of-file flag only when they try to read beyond the last byte, and set the error flag on a device or logical failure.

rows: Returns at end of file or on failure
The character, as an int from 0 to 255
EOF if input ends before the first conversion, else the smaller count / a negative value
count, the number of items requested

Trace (each call stores at most sizeof buf - 1 = 4 characters):
call 1: reads N E P A, buffer full        -> "NEPA"
call 2: reads L and the newline, stops    -> "L\n"

Output (int is 4 bytes): x=15 pos=16 last=15
fwrite 4 ints            file = 5 10 15 20 (16 bytes), pos = 16
fseek(-8, SEEK_END)      pos = 16 - 8 = 8, the start of index 2
fread x                  x = 15, pos = 12
fseek(0, SEEK_CUR)       no move, but required before switching read -> write
fwrite x                 bytes 12..15 overwritten: file = 5 10 15 15
rewind, fread 4 ints     a = 5 10 15 15, pos = 16
Rules that decide whether a positioning or update sequence is valid:
items: In r+, w+ and a+ modes, output may not be followed directly by input without fflush, fseek, fsetpos or rewind in between, and input may not be followed directly by output without a positioning call unless the input reached end of file.
On a text stream, fseek is guaranteed only with offset 0, or with SEEK_SET and a value returned earlier by ftell; arbitrary byte offsets are portable only on binary streams.
Write negative offsets as -(long)sizeof(rec) or -1L * (long)sizeof(rec). The expression -sizeof(rec) is a huge unsigned value, and its conversion to long is not guaranteed to give a negative number.
A successful fseek clears the end-of-file indicator, so reading can resume after a seek even if an earlier read hit the end.
In a and a+ modes every write goes to the current end of the file whatever the position indicator says; reading in a+ mode can happen anywhere.

Strictly, the standard does not require binary streams to support SEEK_END meaningfully, but all mainstream systems do, so fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END) followed by ftell(fp) is the usual way to find a file's size.

concepts.plainText: A positive integer n written with %d takes floor(log10 n) + 1 bytes of text (one more for a minus sign), while fwrite always stores sizeof(int) bytes: with a 4-byte int, 12345 takes 5 bytes as text and 4 bytes in binary.

concepts.text: Common mistakes in file programs:
items: Not testing fopen for NULL and then passing the NULL pointer to fprintf or fgetc, which is undefined behaviour.
Storing fgetc's result in a char, or looping on while (!feof(fp)) instead of testing the value that each read returns.
Forgetting the b on Windows for binary data, so every byte 0x0A written by fwrite gains a 0x0D in front of it and all later record offsets shift.
Opening a file that must be kept with "w", which silently destroys its contents; use "a" or "r+" instead.
Calling fflush(stdin) to discard input: fflush is defined only for output streams.
Mixing up fread's size and count: fread(buf, 1, 40, fp) returns a byte count up to 40, while fread(buf, 40, 1, fp) returns only 0 or 1.

concepts.text: Besides reading and writing, <stdio.h> manages whole files: remove(name) deletes a file and rename(old, new) renames it, both returning 0 on success and nonzero on failure, while tmpfile() creates an anonymous temporary file in "wb+" mode that disappears when it is closed. When an operation fails, ferror(fp) tells a real error apart from end of file (feof), clearerr(fp) resets both flags, and perror("msg") prints msg followed by a description of the error recorded in errno. A robust program checks every fopen, compares every read's return value with what it expected, and checks the result of fclose for output files, because a full disk may be reported only when the buffer is flushed.

For output-prediction questions, track three things line by line: the file's current contents, the position indicator in bytes from 0, and the value each call returns. Remember that fread and fwrite count items, fprintf counts characters, fscanf counts assigned items, and every read moves the position forward by the bytes it consumed.

formulas.plainText: offset of the n-th record (0-based) = n × sizeof(record)
file size in bytes = ftell(fp) after fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END)
number of records = file size ÷ sizeof(record)
EOF = −1; SEEK_SET = 0, SEEK_CUR = 1, SEEK_END = 2

notes.text: while (!feof(fp)) is the classic bug: feof becomes true only after a read fails, so the last record is processed twice. Loop on the return value instead: while (fscanf(...) == 2), while (fgets(...) != NULL), while ((ch = fgetc(fp)) != EOF).

Mode questions hinge on three facts: "r" fails (NULL) if the file does not exist, "w" creates the file and destroys existing contents, "a" creates the file and preserves contents by writing only at the end. The "+" adds the other direction, and "b" switches to binary.
Store the return value of fgetc/getc in an int. If it is stored in a char, EOF (−1) may be indistinguishable from a legitimate byte 0xFF and the loop never ends (or ends early).

fflush is defined only for output streams; fflush(stdin) is undefined behaviour. fclose returns 0 on success, and fopen with a mode such as "rw" is invalid; the valid combinations are r, w, a, r+, w+, a+ with an optional b.

formulas.title: Record offset

formulas.description: Used with fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET) to jump straight to the n-th fixed-length record in a binary file.

formulas.title: File size
formulas.plainText: size = ftell(fp) after fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END)
formulas.description: Moving to the end and reading the position indicator gives the number of bytes in the file.

formulas.title: Record count
formulas.plainText: count = file size / sizeof(record)
formulas.description: The number of fixed-length records stored in a binary file.

formulas.plainText: SEEK_SET = 0, SEEK_CUR = 1, SEEK_END = 2, EOF = −1
formulas.description: The third argument of fseek chooses the reference point; EOF is the value the character and formatted input functions return at end of file.

flashcards.front: Difference between "w" and "a" modes in fopen?
flashcards.back: Both create the file if it is missing, but "w" truncates an existing file to zero length while "a" keeps the contents and forces every write to the end.

flashcards.front: Why should the return value of fgetc be stored in an int?
flashcards.back: fgetc returns either a byte value 0..255 or EOF (−1). Only an int can hold all 257 possibilities; in a char, EOF can collide with a real byte and the loop misbehaves.

flashcards.front: How do you find the size of a file in C?
flashcards.back: fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END); long size = ftell(fp); ftell returns the current byte offset from the start, which at the end equals the file size.

flashcards.front: What are the four arguments of fread and fwrite?
flashcards.back: fread(buffer, size of one item, number of items, fp): the address to fill, the size of each item in bytes, how many items, and the stream. The return value is the number of items done.

questions.questionText: What does fopen() return when the requested file cannot be opened, for example when a file opened in "r" mode does not exist?

Nothing; the program stops with a runtime error
questions.explanation: fopen returns NULL on failure (missing file in read mode, no permission, bad path), so the result must be tested before the stream is used. EOF is what input functions such as fgetc return, not fopen.

questions.questionText: Which fopen() mode opens an existing file for both reading and writing, keeps its contents, and fails (returns NULL) if the file does not exist?
questions.explanation: "r+" requires the file to exist and does not truncate it. "w+" creates or truncates the file, while "a+" creates a missing file and forces every write to the end.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a valid mode string for fopen() in standard C?
questions.explanation: The standard modes are r, w and a, each optionally followed by + and/or b (for example "rb+" or "r+b"). "rw" is not one of them; read-and-write access is requested with "r+".

"r+" opens the existing file without truncating it, with the position at byte 0. Writing XY therefore overwrites a and b in place, leaving XYcdef.
"a+" keeps the existing abc and allows reading anywhere, but every write is forced to the current end of the file, so the fseek to 0 does not change where Z goes. After rewind, fgets reads abcZ.

Whenever any read or write error occurs on fp
Only after an input operation on fp has tried to read past the end of the file
Only after fclose(fp) has been called
questions.explanation: The end-of-file indicator is set by a read that fails at the end; reading the last byte successfully does not set it. That is why while (!feof(fp)) loops run one extra time, and errors are reported separately by ferror.
After 3 is read the newline is still unread, so feof is still 0 and the loop runs once more. That fscanf reaches end of file, returns EOF and leaves x = 3, which is added again: 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9.

fprintf returns the number of characters it wrote, and 42-ab is 5 characters (a negative value would signal an error). It returns neither the number of items converted nor a 0/1 status, and no '\0' is written to the file.
stdout is a FILE * opened automatically, so fputs, fputc and fprintf can all write to it. fputs adds no newline or space, and 'C' - 'A' = 67 - 65 = 2 is printed by %d.

questions.questionText: Which statement about text and binary files is NOT correct?
options: In a binary file of 4-byte int values, the value with index k starts at byte 4k
On Windows, writing '\n' to a text-mode stream stores the two bytes \r\n
fwrite() copies the bytes of a variable to the file exactly as they are stored in memory
Opening a file in "wb" mode makes fprintf(fp, "%d", 1000) store 1000 in its 4-byte internal form
questions.explanation: fprintf always converts values to characters, so 1000 is still written as the four digit characters 1, 0, 0, 0; the b only switches off newline translation. The internal binary form is written with fwrite.
